questions.question: Pack A: 6 eggs for £1.50. Pack B: 15 eggs for £3.30. Which is cheaper per egg?
questions.explanation: A is 25p per egg, B is 22p.

questions.question: Cereal A: 500g for £2.00. Cereal B: 750g for £2.70. Which is better value?
questions.explanation: A is £4.00/kg, B is £3.60/kg.

questions.question: “Was £5, now £3.50.” What's the discount?
A 4-pack of tins costs £4.00, a single tin 95p. Which is cheaper per tin?
questions.explanation: The 4-pack is £1.00 a tin. Multipacks aren't always cheaper.

questions.question: Shampoo: 400ml for £3.60 on “3 for 2”, or 1 litre for £7.50. You need 1.2 litres. Cheapest way?
questions.explanation: 3 for 2 = £7.20 for 1.2 litres. The other way is £11.10.

questions.question: Coffee: a 200g jar for £5.00 or a 750g bag for £16.50. How much do you save per 100g with the bag?
Shrinkflation is when…
options: The pack shrinks but the price stays the same
questions.explanation: The unit price on the shelf label exposes it.

questions.question: 1,000 loyalty points are worth £10 at the till or £30 with a partner. The partner option is worth…
questions.explanation: Partner rewards can multiply your points' value.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Rights Act, you can reject faulty goods for a full refund within…
questions.explanation: You have a 30-day short-term right to reject faulty goods.

questions.question: Buying online from a UK trader, you usually have a cooling-off period of…
questions.explanation: For most online purchases you can cancel within 14 days. Some items, like personalised goods, are excluded.

questions.question: Buy-one-get-one-free is good value only if…
options: You'll actually use both before they go off
questions.explanation: A free item you bin saves nothing.

questions.question: “Up to 70% off” usually means…
questions.explanation: “Up to” means the biggest discount applies to only a few items.

questions.question: Juice: 500ml for £1.75 or 2 litres for £6.00. Which is cheaper per 100ml?
questions.explanation: 35p vs 30p per 100ml.

questions.question: When are supermarket reductions (yellow stickers) usually biggest?
questions.explanation: Prices often drop further towards closing.

questions.question: You buy a £50 supermarket gift card at 4% off via a cashback app, then pay with it and still earn 1 point per £1 (1 point = 1p). Total saved?
questions.explanation: £2 cashback + 50p in points = £2.50.

questions.question: The best way to compare two different pack sizes is:
options: Price per 100g or per unit, shown on the shelf label
questions.explanation: Unit pricing makes different sizes directly comparable.

questions.question: 'Best before' dates tell you about:
options: Quality; food is usually safe after this date if it looks, smells and tastes fine
questions.explanation: Best before is about quality. 'Use by' is about safety and should be respected.

questions.question: Reduced items with yellow stickers are best when:
options: You buy them to freeze or use immediately
They sit in your fridge for a week
You buy them instead of things you need
questions.explanation: Yellow-sticker buys only save money if they get eaten or frozen, not binned.

questions.question: Supermarket own brands are usually:
options: Significantly cheaper, often with similar ingredients, sometimes even made in the same factories
questions.explanation: Own-brand staples are often much cheaper and worth testing before assuming brand is better.

questions.question: Loyalty points are worth the most when:
options: Collected on things you'd buy anyway and redeemed deliberately
You change your shopping to chase points
questions.explanation: Points are a discount on planned spending, not a reason to spend more.

questions.question: A loyalty scheme that raises prices for non-members may mean:
options: The 'discount' is partly just the normal price, so check baseline prices
questions.explanation: Compare member vs non-member prices against other shops to see if the scheme is a real saving.

questions.question: For online orders, UK distance selling rules normally give you:
options: A 14-day cooling-off period to cancel most purchases and return them
questions.explanation: Most online purchases have a 14-day cancellation right from delivery, with some exceptions.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Rights Act, goods must be:
options: As described, of satisfactory quality and fit for purpose
questions.explanation: These are your core statutory rights for goods, on top of any warranty.

questions.question: If an item is faulty, you generally have the strongest position:
options: Within 30 days of purchase, with a short-term right to a full refund
Only with a receipt from the exact till
questions.explanation: The 30-day short-term right to reject gives a full refund; after that, repair or replacement comes first.

questions.question: Between 30 days and 6 months, for a faulty item the burden of proof is:
options: On you to prove it was faulty at delivery
On the retailer to prove the fault wasn't there at delivery
questions.explanation: In the first 6 months it's generally assumed the fault was present unless the retailer proves otherwise.

questions.question: A free trial that needs card details should be:
options: Diarised with a reminder before the charge date, and cancelled if you don't want it
Given a spare card you don't use
questions.explanation: Subscription traps rely on you forgetting; set a reminder before the trial converts.

questions.question: Delivery charges can flip which retailer is cheapest, so you should compare:
options: Item price plus delivery, and returns costs
The checkout total on a different currency
questions.explanation: The real total includes delivery and the realistic cost of a return.

questions.question: Click & collect is often worth considering because:
options: It's frequently free and avoids delivery charges and missed-delivery problems
questions.explanation: Free collection beats a £3-6 delivery fee on small orders.

questions.question: Black Friday deals can be better judged by:
options: Checking the price history, as some 'deals' match or exceed normal prices
questions.explanation: Some sale prices aren't real discounts; price-history tools or your own notes reveal the truth.

questions.question: Refurbished goods from reputable sellers usually come with:
options: A warranty, often 12 months, at a meaningful discount
questions.explanation: Reputable refurb sellers offer warranties and returns, unlike private 'refurb' listings.

questions.question: Buying second-hand from private individuals carries more risk because:
options: Statutory consumer rights don't apply between private sellers
questions.explanation: Private sales lack the Consumer Rights Act, so inspect carefully and pay in protected ways.

questions.question: Price-match promises between supermarkets can save time, but check:
options: The exact terms, like identical items and which competitors qualify
questions.explanation: Price-match schemes have specific rules; they only cover qualifying identical products.

questions.question: 'Multi-buy' offers are worth checking against:
questions.explanation: Multi-buys sometimes cost the same or more than buying singles at their normal price.

questions.question: Cashback and voucher sites save the most when used:
options: On planned purchases, with a quick check before checkout
questions.explanation: The stacking habit matters more than any single deal.

questions.question: A warranty from a manufacturer:
options: Is extra to your statutory rights, which you always keep
questions.explanation: You can't be made to buy an extended warranty to get your statutory rights.

questions.question: Food shopping savings that compound hardest over a year are:
options: Planning meals around what's reduced and in season, cutting waste
questions.explanation: Cutting food waste and planning are the durable wins; single deals are one-offs.
